quote: Gegeb. eine einzige lineare Transformation mit ganzzahligen Coefficienten zwischen $n$ Variablen. Gesucht werden alle ganzen ganzzahligen Funktion, welche [-...-] ungeändert bleiben.
english: Given a single linear transformation with integer coefficients between n variables. Sought are all integral (polynomial) functions with integer coefficients that remain unchanged.
topic: Three short notes: invariants of a single integral linear transformation reduced via canonical form to simultaneous binary invariants; reducing all algebraic equations to simultaneous quadratic equations, so algebraic surfaces come from quadratic forms; and a proposal to express continued fractions and higher continued-fraction algorithms through solutions of differential equations, as sums are approximated by integrals.

triage.modern_statement: Take a single matrix A in GL_n(Z), or more generally an n×n integer matrix. Determine the ring Z[x_1,…,x_n]^A of polynomials with integer coefficients that satisfy f(Ax)=f(x). This is the same as the invariant ring of the cyclic group generated by A. The questions are what this ring looks like, whether it is finitely generated, and how to find generators. The note on the page says the method is to put A into canonical (Jordan) form, so the problem reduces to simultaneous invariants of binary forms. The modern counterpart is the invariants of a single unipotent transformation, equivalently the constants of a Weitzenböck (linear locally nilpotent) derivation. These are known to correspond to joint covariants of binary forms. Part of the original text is struck out or illegible, so the wording of the problem itself is incomplete.
triage.answered_by: R. Weitzenböck answered the central finite-generation question for a single unipotent linear transformation over C: 'Über die Invarianten von linearen Gruppen', Acta Math. 58 (1932), 231–293. C. S. Seshadri gave a proof for any field in J. Math. Kyoto Univ. 1 (1962), 403–409, and A. Tyc gave an elementary proof in Colloq. Math. 78 (1998). The link to classical invariants of binary forms, which is the reduction Hilbert sketched, was developed later, for example by L. Bedratyuk. I found no source that addresses the integer-coefficient (Z) version as Hilbert stated it.

evidence.claim: Classical theorem of Weitzenböck: the algebra of invariants of a single unipotent transformation g in GL_m(K) acting on K[x_1..x_m] is finitely generated.

Weitzenböck's original 1932 proof was for K = C; Seshadri later found a proof for any field. The algebra of constants of a Weitzenböck derivation is the same as the invariants of a single unipotent transformation.
References: Weitzenböck, Acta Math. 58 (1932) 231–293; Seshadri, J. Math. Kyoto Univ. 1 (1962) 403–409; Tyc, elementary proof, Colloq. Math. 78 (1998).
Bedratyuk's work connects Weitzenböck derivations to classical invariant theory of binary forms, using Clebsch's symbolic method.
Seshadri gave a new proof of Weitzenböck's result for the additive group and extended it to positive characteristic.

triage.why: The note asks for the invariants of one linear transformation and proposes reducing them, via canonical form, to simultaneous binary invariants. The closest match in the sources is the theory of invariants of a single unipotent transformation (Weitzenböck derivations). Weitzenböck settled finite generation in 1932, Seshadri extended it in 1962, and the correspondence with joint covariants of binary forms is now standard. Papers on computing these invariants and on generalisations to other algebras appear in arXiv work from 2004 to 2013, which is why I marked the area as still active. The question is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems, although it is closely related to the 14th problem on finite generation. Confidence is medium for three reasons: part of the text is struck out or illegible; Hilbert asked for integer coefficients, and I found no source treating that version directly; and the case of a non-unipotent A of infinite order, and arithmetic questions over Z, were not checked here.
